answers.answer: The arc AB that lies inside angle AMB is the minor arc AB, written $\overset{\frown}{AB}$.
solution: The sides MA and MB of angle AMB cut the circle into two arcs.
The smaller arc, between A and B inside the angle, is the minor arc.
It is written $\overset{\frown}{AB}$.

answers.answer: The arc ACB that lies outside angle AMB, through point C, is the major arc ACB, written $\overset{\frown}{ACB}$.
solution: The sides of angle AMB cut the circle into two arcs.
The larger arc, passing through C, is the major arc.
It is written $\overset{\frown}{ACB}$ (three letters so it is not confused with the minor arc).

answers.answer: The points of arc AB lie inside angle AMB (in its interior, between its two sides).
solution: Arc AB is opposite to the central angle AMB.
Its points lie in the interior of angle AMB, between rays MA and MB.
So arc AB is the minor arc.

answers.answer: The points of arc ACB lie inside the reflex angle AMB, which is outside the angle AMB.
solution: Arc ACB is opposite to the central reflex angle AMB.
Its points lie in the interior of the reflex angle, outside angle AMB.
So arc ACB is the major arc.

answers.answer: AB is a diameter, and arc AB is congruent to arc ACB; each is a semicircle of measure 180°.
solution: If angle AMB is a straight angle, then A, M, B lie on one line.
So AB is a diameter of circle M.
Arc AB and arc ACB are congruent.
Each is called a semicircle, with measure 180°.

answers.answer: No, arc AB is not congruent to arc EF: they have equal measure (50°) but lie in circles of different radii, so arc EF is longer (twice the length of arc AB).
solution: The measure of each arc equals its central angle, so $m(\overset{\frown}{AB}) = m(\overset{\frown}{EF}) = 50^\circ$.
The circles are different (radii 7 cm and 14 cm), so the arcs have different lengths.
Length of $\overset{\frown}{AB}=\frac{50}{360}\times 2\times\frac{22}{7}\times 7$.
Length of $\overset{\frown}{EF}=\frac{50}{360}\times 2\times\frac{22}{7}\times 14$, which is twice as long.
Deduction: equal measure gives equal length only in the same circle (or congruent circles), so the arcs are not congruent.
In circle M, angle AMB and angle CMD are marked equal.
The measure of an arc equals its central angle.
So $m(\overset{\frown}{AB}) = m(\overset{\frown}{CD})$.
The arcs AB and CD have equal measures in the same circle M.
In the same circle, equal arc measures give equal arc lengths.
So the length of $\overset{\frown}{AB}$ = the length of $\overset{\frown}{CD}$.

answers.answer: Draw chords AB and CD in circle M; they are equal in length.
solution: Arcs AB and CD have equal measures in the same circle M.
Draw chord AB joining A and B.
Draw chord CD joining C and D.
By corollary (2), AB = CD.

answers.answer: The minor arc AB is the arc whose points lie inside angle AMB (the smaller arc, less than a semicircle); it is written $\overset{\frown}{AB}$.
The major arc ACB is the larger arc, with its points inside the reflex angle AMB (outside angle AMB), more than a semicircle; it is written $\overset{\frown}{ACB}$ using a third point C.
The points of arc AB lie in the interior of angle AMB (on the circle, between its sides).
The points of arc ACB lie in the interior of the reflex angle AMB, i.e. outside the (non-reflex) angle AMB.
AB is a diameter, so arc AB and arc ACB are congruent; each is a semicircle with measure 180°.

AB and EF are parallel chords.
The arcs between two parallel chords are equal.
The arcs between them are arc FB (left) and arc EA (right).
So m(FB) = m(EA).
The tangent CD is parallel to chord AB.
The arcs between a chord and a parallel tangent are equal.
The arcs between them are arc BC and arc AC.

m(EA) + m(AC) = m(EC), and m(FB) + m(BC) = m(FC).
So m(EC) = m(FC).
m(arc EC) = m(arc FC).
In the same circle, equal arcs have equal chords.
So CE = CF.
